ground_truth_witness:
Witness family: m = 4^k (k >= 1), for which sqrt(m) = 2^k is an exact integer, so every quantity below is computed in exact integer/Fraction arithmetic with no floats.

Master-theorem Case 1 for S(m)=S(m/2)+10 log m (a=1, b=2, m^{log_b a}=m^0=1) requires the hypothesis f(m)=10 log m = O(m^{-eps}) with eps=0.5, i.e. EXISTS c>0, m0 such that FORALL m>=m0: 10 log m <= c * m^{-1/2}, equivalently 10*log(m)*sqrt(m) <= c.

Headline single point, m = 4^40 = 1208925819614629174706176:
  claim says 10*log_2(m)*sqrt(m) <= c; here 10*log_2(m)*sqrt(m) = 879609302220800.
  Concretely f(m) = 10*log_2(m) = 800 while c*m^{-1/2} = c/1099511627776, so f(m) > c*m^{-1/2} for every c <= 879609302220800.
Smaller points in the same family: m=4 gives ratio 40, m=16 gives 160, m=1024 gives 3200, m=4^20 gives 419430400.

Bound-free extension: at m = 4^k the ratio is exactly 20*k*2^k for base-2 logs, and at least L(k) = 6*k*2^k for ANY log base 1 < b <= 10 (using the exact integer fact 2^10 = 1024 > 1000 = 10^3, hence log_b 2 >= log_10 2 > 3/10). L(k) was verified by exact integer comparison to be strictly increasing on k = 1..4000 and satisfies L(k) >= 6*2^k, so it exceeds any constant c at some k with 4^k >= any m0. Therefore no Big-O certificate (c, m0) exists at all -- 10 log m is not O(m^{-0.5}) (it diverges to +infinity while m^{-0.5} -> 0), and Case 1 does not apply.

The concluded answer is also refuted exactly: unrolling on m = 2^k with S(1)=1 and base-2 logs gives the closed form S(2^k) = 1 + 5k(k+1) (>= 1 + 3k(k+1) for any base <= 10): S(2^4)=101, S(2^16)=1361, S(2^32)=5281, S(2^60)=18301. S is strictly increasing and unbounded, so S(m) = Theta(1) is false; the correct order is Theta(log^2 m), obtained from the extended Case 2 since f(m) = Theta(m^{log_2 1} * log m).
ground_truth_flaw: The proof asserts that Master theorem Case 1 applies to S(m)=S(m/2)+10 log m, i.e. that f(m)=10 log m satisfies f(m)=O(m^{log_2 1 - epsilon})=O(m^{-0.5}) with epsilon=0.5, and concludes S(m)=Theta(1).
